question.leadin: Answer the following about famous campaign ads.
question.text: The "Daisy" ad was aired in 1964 by this successor of John F. Kennedy. It depicted a girl counting petals on a daisy, followed by the explosion of a nuclear weapon.
question.answerHtml: Lyndon Baines Johnson [or LBJ; prompt on Johnson alone; do NOT accept or prompt on "Andrew Johnson"]
question.clue: This subject of Robert Caro biographies begun the Head Start school program, and lent his voice to the "Daisy" campaign ad against Barry Goldwater.

swap.leadin: This Supreme Court case overturned the "separate but equal" doctrine of Plessy v. Ferguson.
swap.text: Name this case, in which the Court unanimously ruled that segregation in schools was unconstitutional.
swap.clue: This case's decision cited an experiment in which children were asked to choose between dolls by Kenneth and Mamie Clark.

question.text: The Interstate Highway System was developed during the 1950s under this President, who was inspired by the Autobahn while Supreme Commander of Allied forces during World War II.
question.clue: One of this man's Cabinet members, Charles Wilson, said during confirmation hearings that "for years I thought what was good for the country was good for General Motors."

swap.leadin: This doctrine was established by the Supreme Court in their decision in the 1896 casePlessy v.Ferguson, which considered the legality of a Louisianalaw about streetcar segregation.
swap.text: Name this three-word doctrine. Almost sixty years afterPlessy, this doctrine was partially thrownout in acase against the Topeka Board of Education.
swap.answerHtml: separate but equal (answer must be exact;do not accept or prompt on partial answers)
swap.clue: Brown v. Board of Education overturned Plessy v. Ferguson, which allowed for segregation by establishing this three word doctrine.

question.leadin: Justices Harlan and White both wrote dissents for this case.
question.text: This Supreme Court Case established the need for officers to inform arrestees of their right to an attorney.
question.clue: In a famous partial dissent, Justice Tom C. Clark claimed that the majority opinion in this case went "too far too fast."

swap.text: The White Night Riots took place after the assassination of this first openly gay elected official in the United States, who was shot along with George Moscone by Dan White.
swap.clue: This man's death inspired Cleve Jones to begin the NAMES Project.

question.text: This advocacy group occupied the Pine Ridge Reservation in 1973, leading a 71-day standoff between the group and large amounts of military/paramilitary units. This group also occupied Alcatraz.
question.clue: It composed the Twenty Points during a campaign that ended with an occupation rife with vandalism of a Washington bureaucracy office building.

swap.leadin: This program was inspired by a speech given at the University of Michigan.
swap.text: Name this series of social programs in the 1960s that were part of a "War on Poverty." The Office of Economic Opportunity was created to help enforce this series of programs, which included Head Start and Medicare.
swap.clue: Sargent Shriver helped found a program that focused on early childhood education as part of this initiative, and another of its programs provided health insurance to citizens over the age of 65.

question.text: The March on Washington is best remembered for this famous address by Martin Luther King. Originally titled as the "Normalcy Speech," it is better known by a repeated four-word phrase, and ends with the exhortation "free at last." A
question.answerHtml: “I Have a Dream” [prompt on any answers involving “Normalcy”]
question.clue: The beginning of this speech states that "Five score years ago, a great American, in whose symbolic shadow we stand, signed the Emancipation Proclamation."

swap.text: At the same time, the Bakke decision upheld the constitutionality of this practice of granting special consideration to minorities or members of historically disadvantaged groups.
swap.clue: The University of Michigan's application of this policy was partially upheld in cases named for Lee Bollinger, while the use of a quotas in this policy was outlawed in Regents v Bakke.

question.leadin: Name the following about works of importance in American race relations.
question.text: This author concluded that violence will continue if white America does not change its attitudes towards blacks in The Fire Next Time.

swap.text: Johnson nominated this associate justice to succeed Earl Warren as chief justice in 1968, but a four-day filibuster forced Johnson to withdraw the nomination. He wrote the majority opinion in Tinker v. Des Moines and was Clarence Gideon's lawyer in his appeal to the Supreme Court.
swap.clue: When Lyndon Johnson tried to elevate him to Chief Justice, a filibuster by a bipartisan coalition in the Senate forced the President to withdraw his nomination. He later resigned from the Court after a financial scandal.

question.text: The sit-in was first developed by Bernice Fischer, one of the co-founders of this organization. It was one of the "Big Four" of the civil rights movement along with the SCLC, SNCC ("snick"), and the NAACP.
question.clue: Its second director retired in order to design a planned town called Soul City in North Carolina which quickly fell through.

swap.text: This justice wrote the majority opinion and devised the trimester system developed in Roe.

question.text: Dr. George Gey of Johns Hopkins University discovered that this woman's cells indefinitely reproduce and thus could be used in place of historical experiments. After she died of cervical cancer, this woman's family received no money from biotechnology made from her cells.
question.clue: This woman. Her tumor cells were the first known cells to divide indefinitely, and have since been used extensively in medical research without any compensation to her family.

swap.text: Previous SNCC chairman Stokely Carmichael first popularized this phrase to replace Martin Luther King's "Freedom Now" slogan. This term is often accompanied by raising a closed fist in salute.
swap.clue: This movement's Abeng group formed after Hugh Shearer ordered Mona's campus to expel the New World Group historian who defined its three aims, Walter Rodney.

question.text: This case ruled that using peremptory challenges to exclude potential jurors solely based on race violated the Equal Protection Clause, creating a namesake "challenge" to stop such racial voir dire ("v'wahr deer") machinations.

swap.leadin: During her first congressional race, this big-hat-loving politician used the slogan "This woman's place is in the House-the House of Representatives."
swap.text: Name this feminist politician nicknamed "Battling Bella" who represented Albany in the House for much of the 1970s. She narrowly lost the 1976 New York Senate primary to Daniel Patrick Moynihan.

question.leadin: The Percy Jones Army Hospital in Battle Creek, Michigan, became a federal building complex named for three future senators who met there during World War II, each while receiving treatment for their wounded right arms.
question.text: This man, whose arm had been hit by shrapnel on Utah Beach, became known as the "Conscience of the Senate." He sponsored the Immigration Act of 1965 with Emmanuel Celler.

swap.text: This two-word phrase coined by Senator Harry Byrd Sr. describes an earlier attempt to subvert desegregation in 1950s Virginia. It was aided by the legislative Stanley Plan, which gave white students grants to attend private academies that sprung up, while entire school districts shut down for years as part of this campaign.
swap.clue: As part of this strategy, a state legislature adopted the Stanley Plan, which created a Pupil Placement Board.
